THE COURT
; -
Delivering judgment on the principal and incidental appeals from a judgment
rendered on March 16, 2000 and corrected on April 11, 2000 by the Superior
Court, district of Montreal (the Honourable Luc Lefebvre), condemning the
appellants solidarily liable to pay to each of the respondents the sum of
$10,000 in moral damages and $10,000 in exemplary damages, with interest, the
additional indemnity, and costs.

[
2
]

and deliberating;

[
3
]

[
4
]

the

[
5
]

the

MODIFIES

the conclusions of the judgment so that they read as follows:

the action in part;

the defendants solidarily to
pay to each of the plaintiffs the sum of $75,000 with interest at the legal

In addition,

.

]

______________________________________________________________________

REASONS OF LETARTE J.A.

___________________________________________________________________

[
7
]

The appellants have been ordered to pay each of
the respondents $20,000, namely $10,000 in moral damages and $10,000 in
exemplary damages, following the publication of a text that was held to be
defamatory. Both the appellants and respondents have appealed the decision.

[
8
]

The appellants submit three grounds of appeal:

a)

The trial judge did not apply the proper
criteria when assessing their defence of fair comment;

b)

There are no grounds to award moral damages
since the respondents have renounced to them by undertaking to donate the net
amount of the compensation awarded to charitable organizations;

c)

There are no grounds to award damages, since the
appellants expressed an opinion that was honest, sincere, and of public
interest.

[
9
]

The respondents, for their part, claim that the
compensation awarded is so out of proportion to the circumstances of the case
that the intervention of the Court of Appeal is warranted on the issue of
damages, both moral and exemplary.

[
10
]

In my view, a detailed examination of the
evidence summarized by the trial judge, along with the principles of civil law
applicable to the present case as recently defined by the Supreme Court in
Prud’homme
,
[1]
prohibit this Court from intervening on the
issue of the appellants’ liability. I believe, however, that certain important
factors were omitted from the trial judge’s assessment of non-pecuniary
damages, moral damages or those resulting from loss of reputation, as well as
exemplary or punitive damages. This constitutes a palpable and overriding error
that justifies a considerable increase in the amount of damages awarded.

THE FACTS

[
11
]

The parties do not dispute the facts. I refer to
the trial judge’s narration of events:

[
translation
]

[3] In January 1993, Mr. Jacques
Parizeau was president of the Parti Québécois and Leader of the Opposition in
the National Assembly, while Lucien Bouchard was leader of the Bloc Québécois
and Member of Parliament in the House of Commons.

[4] Mr. Richard Lafferty, a
financial analyst, has been director of the investment consultant firm
Lafferty, Harwood for approximately thirty years. This firm publishes a monthly
investment analysis report aimed at its 275 clients, all business people who
pay an annual fee of $10,000 to receive it. This report is confidential and
contains a notice to this effect.
[2]

[5] The report itself is divided
into different sections. The first contains an analysis of the political
situation prevailing in Quebec
and the rest of Canada. The
second provides an analysis of general economic conditions and comments on the
principal industrial sectors. The subsequent sections contain detailed analyses
of the best stocks to own in various economic sectors.

[6] In January 1993, Mr. Robert
Bourassa was still premier of Quebec, although since his cancer had come out of remission, he was
obliged to travel to the United States to undergo new treatment. Mr. Brian Mulroney was expected to retire
from politics soon. This was the context in which Mr. Lafferty wrote his
political analysis in the January 1993 issue of the report. The extracts that
have given rise to the current dispute are reproduced below:

The Premier
is considering further treatment at the National Institute of Health in
Bethesda
, Maryland.

…

… while under this treatment it is unlikely that Premier Bourassa could
be politically active. This would create a political vacuum which the
nationalists led by Jacques Parizeau are naturally anxious to engulf.

…

The
Quebec
scene is more serious, particularly if
Premier Bourassa were to be absent. It is serious from the viewpoint that the
leading contending party is based on demoguery
[3]

which has as its fountain of political rhetoric the dominating theme of
nationalism.

Nationalism is the equivalent of tribalism and is amongst the most
primitive forms of any human society. It is prevalent through most countries of

Africa
and inevitably results in a dictatorship because the
concepts of democracy are overridden by collective emotionalism. It cannot be
otherwise.

Jacques Parizeau, the leader of the Parti Québécois at the provincial
level, and Lucien Bouchard, the leader of the Bloc Québécois at the federal
level, aim their appeal entirely at nationalism. It is a classic form of
demoguery and is no different from what Hitler did although Hitler at the time
was operating in a greater political vacuum than that which presently prevails
in
Quebec
or
Canada
,
although with the financial pressures developing both constituencies are coming
into a political inoperative environment.

If
people, because it gives them a sense of security and an emotional
satisfaction, want to engage in nationalism and become the subjects of
demagogues, that is their choice. What is interesting is after a long period of
what might be termed crude democracy, the collective trend in the Province of Quebec should be in this
direction and that there is no organized hard core within the population that
is willing to stand up and show how shallow the political thesis is.
There
are no organized patriots in
Quebec
with the concepts of liberty, equality, and paternity
[4]

The
same situation prevailed with Hitler
. The large
industrialists and the banks did not wish to offend the dictatorial leadership
for fear of punitive retaliation and that today seems largely the situation in
the Province of Quebec.

The
Chairman of the Royal Bank of Canada at the time of the Referendum last October predicted economic ruin
if the Charlottetown accord
failed.

He was
strongly criticized by the leader of the Parti-Québécois for the bank's report
"Unity or Disunity: The Benefits and the Costs". It comprised 47
pages.

In the
report the Bank contended that if the "No" vote were to win the
referendum, Quebec would leave
confederation. The report predicted if that were to happen, inflation would
triple and a further 800,000 Canadians would become unemployed.

The
report went on the predict that by the year 2000 the standard of living of
Canadians would drop by 20%; family income would drop by $10,000 and one
million Canadians would move south.

As a
result of publishing the report, the Royal Bank lost $100 million in deposits
essentially as a consequence of demoguery.

We
too will probably be punitized for expressing these views but Hitler's success
was based entirely on fear and these are the tactics of the Parti-Québécois
.

(Emphasis added)

[7] On February 9, a journalist
from Le Devoir who had received a copy of this report published certain
extracts on the first page with the title “Bouchard, Parizeau, Hitler: même
combat.” ([
translation
]
“Bouchard, Parizeau, Hitler: The Same Struggle.”)

[8] Mr. Parizeau and Mr. Bouchard
said that when they became aware of this article, they were profoundly hurt and
indignant. They therefore decided to launch a suit in defamation against both
Mr. Lafferty and Lafferty, Harwood.

[9] In the following days,
editorial writers in the major Quebec newspapers condemned Mr. Lafferty’s remarks, as did the Human
Rights League and B’nai Brith Canada.

[10] On February 16, Mr. Lafferty
repeated the same remarks in a letter addressed to his clients. He also sent a
copy to the media.

[11] On February 19, Mr. Parizeau
and Mr. Bouchard launched their action.

JUDGMENT

Liability

[
12
]

The trial judge immediately recognized that the
impugned texts were defamatory because they were likely to expose the
respondents to hatred and contempt and to have an impact upon their reputation.

[
13
]

It cannot be disputed that comparing the
respondents to Hitler represents one of the most serious attacks that could
ever be launched on their dignity and reputation. It is therefore not
surprising that the judge’s first conclusion on the facts was not contested by
the appellants, who plead only the defence of fair comment.

[
14
]

Relying on
Steenhaut v. Vigneault
[5]
and
Picard v. Gros-Louis
,
[6]
the trial judge summarized the three
elements characterizing the nature of the fair comment defence as follows:

1.

The comment must be on a matter of public
interest;

2.

The comment must be made with the honest intent
to serve a just cause;

3.

The comment represents a reasonably sustainable
conclusion in view of the reported facts.

[
15
]

On numerous occasions since the judgments cited
in the preceding paragraphs, this Court has reaffirmed that these three
conditions must be present.
[7]

[
16
]

The trial judge recognized that the report
addressed an issue of public interest and that the appellants had the honest
intention to serve a just cause. However, he also concluded that in addition to
being defamatory, the appellants’ remarks were false and that they did not
express reasonably justifiable conclusions given the facts reported.

[
17
]

According to the trial judge, the text at issue
compared the political activities of the respondents to those of Hitler on
three occasions. He stated as follows:

[
translation
]

-

First, he (the appellant) emphasized that the
political activities of the leaders of the Parti Québécois and the Bloc
Québécois rely on an appeal to the nationalist emotions of the Québécois
people. For him, nationalism is equivalent to tribalism which inevitably leads
to dictatorship. It is a classic form of demagoguery comparable to Hitler’s;

-

Later on, the author points out that there are
no organized patriotic groups in Quebec founded on the concepts of liberty, equality, and fraternity that
are able to counter this appeal to nationalism. The same situation existed
under Hitler, under whose regime banks and big business avoided offending the
dictatorial leadership for fear of reprisals. The same situation prevails in Quebec; and

-

Finally, the financial analyst concluded that
his firm would probably be penalized because he had expressed his opinions. He
concluded that Hitler’s success was based on fear and that the same tactics
were used by the Parti Québécois.

[
18
]

After analyzing the text and all of the
evidence submitted, in particular the testimony of Mr. Lafferty during
examination on discovery and the admissions of the parties regarding the
horrors and atrocities committed by Hitler, the trial judge said that he [
translation
] “
had
no hesitation in concluding that the remarks made by Mr.
Lafferty regarding the plaintiffs are
false and defamatory
.”

[
19
]

After this finding of fact, he added:

[
translation
]

The appellant was unable to provide
concrete examples when called upon to do so, just as he was unable to establish
any facts that would lead to the conclusion that the respondents were defending
antidemocratic or racist principles, or that they wanted to restrict the
fundamental freedoms of citizens or certain categories thereof.

[
20
]

Then, proposing the objective test of the
reasonable reader, he concluded that this reader would understand the
following, at the very least, from the text:

[
translation
]

-

That the [respondents] are nationalists and that
their political activities, like Hitler’s, will lead inevitably to
dictatorship;

-

That their demagogic statements cause fear and
no one dares criticize them for fear of reprisal; and

-

That they employ the same fear tactics as Hitler.

ANALYSIS

[
21
]

The cases from this Court cited by the trial
judge
[8]

describe a conflict between two fundamental rights that are guaranteed in the
constitution and the
Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms
.
[9]
The first is freedom of speech, a basic
pillar of our democracy, which is tempered by the second, the right of each
citizen to his or her honour, dignity, and reputation. Each extends only as far
as it does not infringe on the other.

[
22
]

In
Prud’homme
,
[10]
L’Heureux-Dubé and LeBel JJ. described the
opposition between freedom of speech and the right to dignity and reputation as
follows:

43. [F]reedom of speech is not
absolute. It is limited by,
inter alia
, the requirements imposed by
other people's right to the protection of their reputation. As Cory J. observed
in
Hill
,
[11]
reputation is an
attribute of personality that any democratic society concerned about respect
for the individual must protect.

Democracy has always recognized and
cherished the fundamental importance of an individual. That importance must, in
turn, be based upon the good repute of a person. It is that good repute which
enhances an individual's sense of worth and value. False allegations can so
very quickly and completely destroy a good reputation. A reputation tarnished
by libel can seldom regain its former lustre. A democratic society, therefore,
has an interest in ensuring that its members can enjoy and protect their good
reputation so long as it is merited.

44.     The
right to reputation is also protected, in Quebec, by
s. 4
of the
Charter of
Human Rights and Freedoms
and by
art. 3

C.C.Q.
As well, although it
is not specifically mentioned in the
Canadian Charter
, the good
reputation of the individual represents and reflects the innate dignity of the
individual, a concept which underlies all the
Canadian Charter
rights (
Hill
[12]
).

[
23
]

In
Savard
,
[13]
Rousseau-Houle J.A. made similar
observations:

[
translation
]

[31] The freedom of speech
entrenched in the constitution and guaranteed in the
Quebec Charter of Human
Rights and Freedoms
is fundamental to our society.
[14]
A diversity of ideas and opinions is
inherently beneficial to the community and the individual. Without this freedom
to express ideas and to criticize the operation of institutions or the conduct
of individual members of government agencies, democratic forms of government
could not survive.
[15]

[32] Freedom of speech has never
been recognized as an absolute right, however. In cases of defamation or libel,
the twin values of reputation and freedom of speech will clash. False and
defamatory statements are very tenuously related to the core values that
underlie freedom of expression. As Cory J. stated in
Hill
,
[16]
false and defamatory statements cannot
enhance development of the individual, and they undermine healthy participation
in the affairs of the community.

[
24
]

In her analysis of the allegation of fair
comment, she distinguishes between a statement of fact and comment or criticism
itself, bringing the analysis of this defence within our own civilian
framework, founded on fault, injury, and causation. She emphasizes that
criteria drawn from the Common law may [
translation
]
“
serve as a guide to help the courts determine
whether the civil fault of defamation exists
.”

[
25
]

She writes:

[
translation
]

[39] This defence applies only to
comments and not to statements of fact. In the latter case, the person who has
made the defamatory remarks may succeed in the defence by proving the truth of
the facts on which he or she is relying. The person cannot simply allege good
faith or claim an honest belief in something another person has said.
[17]

[40] Distinguishing between a
statement of fact and an opinion is sometimes difficult to do. Indeed, Forget
J.A. noted in
Société Radio-Canada v. Moncef Guitouni
[18]
that he did not see why it was necessary
to say that a report is either uniquely factual or uniquely an expression of
opinion. In reality, the two concepts are intermixed, since the facts must be
presented before opinions are expressed.

[41] Nevertheless, the distinction
must be made if a defendant wishes to use the defence of fair comment. To
determine whether something is a statement of fact or an opinion, we must place
the defamatory remarks in their context and ask ourselves how a reasonable
person would consider these remarks. Brown
[19]

expresses it in the following manner:

Would an ordinary
person, reading the matter complained of, be likely to understand it as an
expression of the writer’s opinion or as a declaration of an existing fact?

[
26
]

We will now turn to how the trial judge dealt
with the appellants’ defence:

[
translation
]

[69] The real issue before the
Court is whether the third condition has been respected, that is, whether Mr.
Lafferty’s remarks were
reasonably sustainable
.

[70] This Court was surprised to
see how little Mr. Lafferty actually knew about Hitler. He has never read any
biographies of him, nor has he read
Mein

Kampf
.
[20]
He does not know the contents of the book.
He did not know that Hitler had been democratically elected.
[21]

[71] What knowledge he did have of
Hitler he gained by taking part in World War II and reading the newspapers of
the day as well as other biographies, such as those of Churchill or Eisenhower.

[22]
Indeed, he remarked at the hearing:

“I haven’t
been studying Hitler for the forty years, fifty years.”
[23]

[72] As for the program of the
Parti Québécois, he has never read it. He has read only summaries in the
newspapers.
[24]

[73] Furthermore, he acknowledges
that he has read no documents giving the positions of Mr. Bouchard and Mr.
Parizeau on human rights and freedoms and those of minorities. Nevertheless, he
says he knows Mr. Parizeau personally and has read the English-language version
of Mr. Bouchard’s biography. However, this was published only in 1994. The
Court therefore concludes that he had not read it in January 1993, the date of
the defamatory publication.

[74] It is clear from the evidence
that before comparing the political activities of the plaintiffs with those of
Hitler, the defendant Lafferty had not done any research, taken any steps, or
verified his information. We cannot even say that his research was half-baked,
since he did no research at all. He relied on his impressions and what he
remembered of Hitler’s political activities, even though he had not studied
these actions for more than 40 or 50 years.

[75] The Court is of the opinion
that Mr. Lafferty has not met the burden of establishing that his remarks of
January 1993 were reasonably sustainable. Therefore, his defence of fair
comment must fail.

[
27
]

The appellants maintain that the standard
of the reasonableness of the remarks no longer applies. They express their
disagreement thus:
“We submit respectfully, however,
that the third criterion, as stated above, is no longer a correct statement of
law.”

They are wrong.

[
28
]

Prud’homme
[25]
brings us back
to the special nature of Quebec civil law in matters of liability, that is, to
the idea of fault. We must therefore conclude that the unreasonable nature of a
defamatory remark is one element that can demonstrate a lack of respect for the
rules of conduct of a prudent and diligent person.

[
29
]

This judgment reminds us that the defence of honest and fair comment
was introduced under the influence of a
tendency
in Quebec courts to “
import common law concepts in
areas of the law that are governed by both public law and private law rules,
”
pointing out that “
whether they may be raised
depends on whether they are public in nature
.”

[
30
]

After referring to the analysis by Professor
Côté,
[26]

L’Heureux-Dubé and LeBel JJ. distinguish actions in defamation under the Common
law from those under the
Civil Code
. While the first are essentially founded on
rules of liability that come into play as soon as it is shown that the
published texts are defamatory, the law in Quebec follows other rules: “
the civil law rules governing defamation actions are based
on the concept of fault
.”

[
31
]

They write:

[58] As a result of the mechanism
that it implies and the basic idea that underlies it, that is, the existence of
a presumption of malice, the defence of qualified privilege cannot be
incorporated in that form into the civil law rules which are based on a
presumption of good faith, without disturbing the coherence of its application
in the area of public authority liability. Moreover, bad faith or malice need
not be established in order for fault to be proved in the civil law: liability
may result from an act of negligence, in which case the
defamation
is a
quasi-delict. Accordingly, permitting the defence of qualified privilege to be
incorporated into the civil law would amount to reducing defamation, as it is
understood in the civil law, to its delictual dimension alone, thereby
stripping it of its important quasi-delictual dimension (Gaudreault-Desbiens,
supra
,
at p. 500).

[59] To avoid that result, while
still using legal techniques that are consistent with the methods of the civil
law, simply importing qualified privilege does not seem to be the desirable or
necessary solution. What we must first determine is whether the Quebec law of
civil liability includes rules that are capable of providing equivalent
protection to an elected municipal official, and of preserving the societal
values and interests that the rule of qualified privilege that applies to an
elected municipal official in the common law is intended to preserve. This
approach to transposition is based, in this case, on the fact that the concept
of fault in Quebec civil law is a flexible one. However, the legal
characterization of the conduct, which is
based on an objective examination
of reasonable conduct
, is still determined from the context. This makes it
possible to take into consideration the situation of the person who committed
the impugned act, and incorporate the values and interests that will be used to
determine, when the analysis has been completed, whether a civil fault has been
committed. It can be concluded, from the facts that fault is determined from
the context and that there is a presumption of good faith, that the application
of the rules of the law of civil liability will protect the interests and
values that the law respecting public authorities seeks to protect when it
defines the status of an elected municipal official. In other words, the
defence of qualified privilege has an equivalent in the civil law, and,
moreover, that defence must be applied in accordance with the legislative
intent expressed in art. 1376
C.C.Q.

…

(Emphasis added)

[
32
]

They continue:

[62] The problems that often arise
when this defence has been asserted in the courts in Quebec were again in
evidence in the recent decision of the Quebec Court of Appeal in
Hervieux-Payette,
supra
. In that case, which involved a
defamation
suit, the majority
of the Court of Appeal placed its analysis in the civil law context at the
outset, based on the concept of fault, and also referring, on that point, to
the trial judgment (see p. 1673, para. 14). Later, however, the majority
reasons examined the defence of fair comment without any apparent connection to
the concept of fault, although that concept was the underpinning of its
analysis.
Terminological uncertainty and ambiguity, if not ambiguity in the
legal concepts, could be avoided by focusing the analysis more on the
objective, although still context-based, nature of the concept of civil fault.
This avoids the risk of forgetting that the reasonableness standard is not
parallel to or concurrent with the standard set out in art. 1457
C.C.Q.

for evaluating conduct. The standard of what is reasonable, rather, is central
to art. 1457
C.C.Q.
, which refers to it for the purpose of determining
whether the conduct in issue adheres to the standard of the reasonable person,
acting in a particular context. Reasonableness serves as a method for making a
legal assessment of the conduct in order to determine whether it must be
legally characterized as a fault.
As we shall now see, the fact that this
is a system of liability based on the establishment of fault means that
contextual factors that the defence of "fair comment" attempts to
incorporate into the legal rules governing
defamation
may be taken into
consideration.

(Emphasis added)

[
33
]

This leads them to conclude that:

[63] …It therefore serves no
purpose to mechanically apply the criteria for the defence of fair comment. At
the risk of repetition, the rules of civil liability are flexible and require
that whether a fault has been committed be determined by examining all of the
circumstances.

[
34
]

Prud’homme

instructs that we must analyze whether remarks are defamatory according to an
objective standard, leading me to conclude, given my interpretation of articles
1053
C.C.L.C.
and 1457
C.C.Q.,
that the good faith of the
negligent writer does not shelter him from liability for the damages he has
caused.

[
35
]

This principle is set out in the following
extracts from
Prud’homme
:

[34] Whether remarks are defamatory
is determined by applying an objective standard (
Hervieux-Payette v. Société
Saint-Jean-Baptiste de Montréal
,
1997 CanLII 8276 (QC CS)
, [1998] R.J.Q. 131 (Sup. Ct.), at p. 143,
reversed on other grounds by
Société Saint-Jean-Baptiste de Montréal v.
Hervieux-Payette
,
2002 CanLII 8266 (QC CA)
, [2002] R.J.Q. 1669 (C.A.)). In other words, we must ask
whether an ordinary person would believe that the remarks made, when viewed as
a whole, brought discredit on the reputation of another person. On this point,
we should note that words may be defamatory because of the idea they expressly
convey, or by the insinuations that may be inferred from them. In
Beaudoin
v. La Presse Ltée
,
1997 CanLII 8365 (QC CS)
, [1998] R.J.Q. 204 (Sup. Ct.), at p. 211, Senécal J.
provided a good summary of the approach to be taken in determining whether
particular remarks are defamatory in nature:

[
translation
] "The
form in which the libel is expressed is of little import; it is the result
achieved in the mind of the reader that creates the delict." The
defamatory allegation or imputation may be direct, or it may be indirect,
"by simple allusion, insinuation or irony, or be made conditionally, as an
expression of doubt, or hypothetically." Often, the allegation or
imputation "is conveyed to the reader by way of a simple insinuation, an
interrogative sentence, a reference to a rumour, mention of information that
has infiltrated the public awareness, juxtaposition of unrelated facts that,
together, take on the appearance of being related".

The words must also be interpreted
in their context. For instance, "it is not possible to isolate a passage
from a text and complain of it, if the entire text sheds a different light on
that excerpt". On the other hand, "it matters little that the
elements of which it is composed are true if the text as a whole conveys a
message that is contrary to reality". In fact, truth or reality may be distorted
by half-truths, selective compilation, omissions, and so on. "We must
consider a newspaper article or radio broadcast as a whole, and the sentences
and words must be interpreted by reference to one another."

[35]   However, a
person who has made remarks that are deemed to be defamatory will not
necessarily be civilly liable for them. The plaintiff must further demonstrate
that the person who made the remarks committed a wrongful act. In
La
responsabilité civile
(5th ed. 1998), at pp. 301-2, J.-L. Baudouin and P.
Deslauriers point out that in defamation cases, the wrongful act may derive

In

,
[37]

the general principles for assessing punitive damages are defined as follows:

Punitive damages may be awarded in
situations where the defendant's misconduct is so malicious, oppressive and
high-handed that it offends the court's sense of decency. Punitive damages bear
no relation to what the plaintiff should receive by way of compensation. Their
aim is not to compensate the plaintiff, but rather to punish the defendant. It
is the means by which the jury or judge expresses its outrage at the egregious
conduct of the defendant. They are in the nature of a fine which is meant to
act as a deterrent to the defendant and to others from acting in this manner.
It is important to emphasize that punitive damages should only be awarded in
those circumstances where the combined award of general and aggravated damages would
be insufficient to achieve the goal of punishment and deterrence.

Unlike compensatory damages,
punitive damages are not at large. Consequently, courts have a much greater
scope and discretion on appeal. The appellate review should be based upon the court's
estimation as to whether the punitive damages serve a rational purpose. In
other words, was the misconduct of the defendant so outrageous that punitive
damages were rationally required to act as deterrence?

This was the test formulated by
Robins J.A. in
Walker v. CFTO Ltd
.
[38]

In that case, he found that the general damages award of $908,000 was obviously
sufficient to satisfy whatever need there was for punishment and deterrence. He
found that, in those circumstances, the $50,000 punitive damage award served no
rational purpose. The Court of Appeal, in the case at bar, applied the same
reasoning and upheld the award of punitive damages.

Punitive damages can and do serve a
useful purpose. But for them, it would be all too easy for the large, wealthy
and powerful to persist in libelling vulnerable victims. Awards of general and
aggravated damages alone might simply be regarded as a licence fee for
continuing a character assassination.
The protection of a person's
reputation arising from the publication of false and injurious statements must
be effective. The most effective means of protection will be supplied by the
knowledge that fines in the form of punitive damages may be awarded in cases
where the defendant's conduct is truly outrageous.

The very recent decision by the Supreme Court of Canada in
Prud’homme
v. Prud’homme

urges courts that must apply the

to refrain from

L’Heureux-Dubé and LeBel JJ. described the major differences separating these

[55]

The common law rules governing
actions in defamation are essentially based on the rules of strict liability.
The plaintiff is not required to establish wrongdoing on the part of the
defendant. The plaintiff's only burden of proof is to establish that the words
spoken by the defendant were of such a nature as to bring the plaintiff's
reputation into disregard. In comparison, the civil law rules governing
defamation actions are based on the concept of fault. To succeed, as we saw
earlier, the plaintiff must establish not only that the defendant uttered the
offensive words about him or her, but also that the defendant committed a fault
in so doing.

…

…For
reasons relating to the process followed by an action for defamation in the

civil liability. …

[Citations omitted]

[

The Supreme Court stresses that the system governing liability in
the civil law proceeds in an inverse fashion from the Common law recourse in

once the plaintiff establishes that the

.”
[56]

[

As the Supreme Court reminds us,

ANALYSIS

[
130
]

The Supreme Court defines defamation in the
following terms:
[66]

Defamation consists in the
communication of spoken or written remarks that cause someone to lose in
estimation or consideration, or that prompt unfavourable or unpleasant feelings
toward him or her.

[
131
]

This definition seems more expansive than the popular definitions of
the word as they appear in contemporary dictionaries:

Le Petit Robert 1:
[67]

[TRANSLATION]

Any allegation or imputation of
fact that injures the honour or the consideration of the person or group to
which the fact is imputed.

Larousse Sélection:
[68]

[
translation
]

Allegation of a fact that by its
nature injures the honour or consideration of a person.

[
132
]

As is apparent, these definitions seem to limit defamation to
statements of fact, while the definition accepted by the Supreme Court, by
using “
spoken or written remarks
”, does not
exclude characterizations of fact. In short, the Supreme Court’s approach goes
beyond mere semantics and includes more insidious cases where the injury takes
the form of the expression of an opinion.

[
133
]

In light of the definition provided in
Prud’homme
, I must
conclude that the comparison made by Lafferty is defamatory because it can
cause the respondents to lose the esteem or consideration they normally enjoy
or, at the very least, prompt unfavourable or unpleasant feelings toward them.

[
134
]

On the other hand, it should be remembered that the existence of
defamatory remarks does not necessarily mean the existence of a civil fault:
[69]

However, a person who has made
remarks that are deemed to be defamatory will not necessarily be civilly liable
for them. The plaintiff must further demonstrate that the person who made the
remarks committed a wrongful act.

[
135
]

In the present case, I feel it is of primary importance to remember
that the trial judge concluded that the appellant was honest and sincere:

[
translation
]

In the present case, the Court also
considers that Mr. Lafferty sincerely believes what he wrote and that he felt
it was his obligation to share this with his clients.

[
136
]

This conclusion, which is not contested by the respondents, moves
the characterization of the wrongfulness of the act away from malice into the
area of negligence or recklessness. If the appellant sincerely believed in the
accuracy of what he was writing, must we find him liable because he acted
recklessly or carelessly? The answer to this question depends first and
foremost on how the impugned remarks are characterized. Are they statements of
fact, the expression of an opinion, or a subtle mixture of the two?

[
137
]

In the first case, the inaccuracy or falsity of the remarks can be
of great weight in determining whether there was negligence or recklessness.
The analysis of the context and the circumstances will therefore bear on not
only whether it was appropriate to disseminate the statements of fact, whether they
be true or false, but also on what kind of precautions the author took to
verify the accuracy of his statements once they were shown to be false.

[
138
]

In contrast, in the second case, the truth or falseness of the
remark is not relevant since, by definition, an opinion is a state of mind that
cannot be characterized as either true or false.  It is difficult for an
opinion to be either accurate or inaccurate. At the most, we may conclude that
it is not well-founded because of certain weaknesses in its intellectual
underpinnings. The analysis of the context and circumstances of how an opinion
is expressed will focus more on the appropriateness of the content of the
remark than on whether it is true or false.

[
139
]

There is more, however. Because we cannot judge opinions before they
are expressed, we tend too often to forget that, on an independent basis, they
too have the status of a fundamental freedom, and as such benefit from specific
legal protection. In theory, at least, freedom of opinion is distinct from
freedom of expression, which is a more general concept applying to a large
number of human activities.
[70]
Not
all these activities can be individually characterized as being in the category
of a fundamental freedom, and it is only under the aegis of expression that
they can be protected by the Charters. Thus, no one enjoys the fundamental
right to make a pornographic drawing, but it is conceivable, depending on the
context and circumstances, that such an activity may benefit from the immunity
conferred through freedom of expression. This is the same type of protection
that the
Quebec
Charter
[71]

confers on statements of fact.

[
140
]

Freedom of opinion, for its part, is conceived differently, because,
fundamentally, each citizen has the right to form an opinion before he or she
expresses it. When, for practical purposes, freedom of opinion is grouped
together with freedom of expression, it must be done by keeping in mind that
citizens enjoy much greater latitude in expressing an opinion than in
expressing a fact. In other words, the right to freedom of expression protected
by the Charters has a broader scope when it protects an opinion, and whether or
not the statement of an opinion is a fault cannot be measured according to the
same scale as a statement of fact. In terms of the test of the appropriateness
of the content of the remark, a fault is committed when there is abuse, but in
the case of a statement of opinion, the scope of what is permitted is much
broader than when the remarks are statements of facts.

[
141
]

In hybrid cases, where the statement contains both fact and opinion,
the analytical criteria for the first two categories are both applied.

[
142
]

Frequently, the opinion expressed is anchored by a factual basis
that may be revealed to be false, and this in turn can have a determinative
influence on whether the reproached act is considered a fault. Fault can also
flow from the inappropriateness of expressing the fact at issue.

[
143
]

From another perspective, the inferences from the facts drawn by the
author of the statement are in the realm of opinion. They therefore must meet
the test of appropriateness in its widest sense when it comes to determining,
as a last resort, whether there has been an abuse in the exercise of the rights
protected by the Charters.

[
144
]

As Rousseau-Houle J.A. recently pointed out in
Radiomutuel inc.
v. Savard
,
[72]
it is
sometimes difficult to make a precise distinction between an opinion and a
statement of fact. The reaction of a reasonable person who becomes aware of
defamatory remarks is the most reliable test with which to measure the relative
degrees of factual and descriptive content of a remark:
[73]

Would an ordinary person, reading
the matter complained of, be likely to understand it as an expression of the
writer's opinion or as a declaration of an existing fact?

[
145
]

The trial judge, for his part, stated that Lafferty’s remarks [
translation
]
“are untruthful and defamatory”
. In so doing, he
assessed them as though they were pure statements of fact, which, with respect,
I consider to be incorrect.

[
146
]

In my opinion, Lafferty’s remarks fall under the third category,
that of hybrid cases, since the comparison drawn between the respondents and
Adolf Hitler rests on a factual basis. However, it is important to measure
precisely the respective importance of the factual and descriptive content in
the text as a whole.

[
147
]

The impugned remarks are found in a section of the report that is
clearly editorial. They cannot be isolated from the whole, which is a vast
critique of our parliamentary system. The author gives vent to his
frustrations, broadly distributing blame and unpleasant descriptions. The
respondents are not the only persons attacked, although they are more clearly
identified than most of the other targets.

[
148
]

In my opinion, the attention of the reasonable person to whom these
remarks are addressed, namely the subscriber to the Lafferty Canadian Report,
is mainly focused on the opinions expressed; the reader would tend to see only
the expression of a personal opinion rather than a statement of fact.
Therefore, to determine whether or not the remarks are abusive, the analysis
must specifically address the standard of appropriateness in its broad sense.
Of course, this focus does not exclude an examination of the truthfulness of
the factual content.

[
149
]

In this case, the scope of the latter examination is limited to the
basic facts from which Lafferty extrapolates. These include, for example, the
fact that the Parti Québécois and the Bloc, led by the respondents Parizeau and
Bouchard, respectively, are political organizations that advocate nationalism;
that the German National Socialist Party, led by Hitler, also advocated
nationalism; that there were rumours of the imminent departure of Prime
Minister Mulroney; and that Premier Bourassa was suffering from a serious illness.
No one is questioning the truth of these basic facts, although many may deplore
the cruel lack of subtlety they display. But in this case, this lack does not
come from a desire to suppress facts that others would consider essential;
rather, it is due to the observer’s perspective on the situation. It is very
clear from Lafferty’s remarks that he sees the defects of nationalism as so
dominant that this alone is justification for comparing those who share this
political position. The lack of nuance is, in short, a result of the great
weight Lafferty assigns to the elements he believes are relevant. I conclude
that the factual content of the text, as bare as it may be, meets the test of
truthfulness.

[
150
]

The more problematic elements, those giving rise to the respondents’
indignation and the harsh disapproval of many observers, are in reality the
characterizations and inferences Lafferty draws from the facts, which basically
are not inaccurate. As previously noted, whether or not the text at issue
constitutes a fault must be evaluated primarily according to its degree of
appropriateness, taking into account the context and the circumstances as a
whole.

[
151
]

First and foremost, it must be remembered that the impugned opinion
relates to a matter of public interest and that, in the circumstances, it is
relevant to the legitimate objectives of the report, which is to expose
subscribers to the views of the firm on subjects likely to influence their
financial decisions. Seen from this perspective, the expression of Lafferty’s
opinion was not gratuitous since the political context he discussed is a matter
likely to preoccupy investors. Indeed, the judge believed the appellant when
the latter declared that he felt it was his duty to inform his clients of his
opinion on the political situation prevailing at the time. Prima facie, when
Lafferty’s actions are considered from this perspective, his remarks meet the
test of general appropriateness, with respect to both their factual and
editorial content.

[
152
]

In addition, it is my view that Lafferty’s act must be characterized
as participation in the democratic debate. It matters little that the author of
the impugned text is not someone engaged in politics. By definition, the
political arena accepts all players, even those who prefer only selective
participation, and the democratic debate draws participants from private homes
as well as from television studios. In short, it is the content of the remarks
and the context in which they were made that allow us to evaluate them in this
way. In my view, such a characterization is necessary, not only because of the
subject discussed but also because of the editorial environment in which the
remarks were made.

[
153
]

Nor should we underestimate the importance of the fact that the
opinion Lafferty expressed bears on a matter of critical importance to the
democratic debate, namely the major policy positions held by those who may possibly
take over the reins of power.

[
154
]

In a number of analogous cases the Supreme Court has held that the
freedoms of opinion and expression recognized by the
Canadian

Charter
[74]
and the
Quebec
Charter
[75]
are fundamental in their very nature:

Irwin Toy v. Quebec (A.G.)
:
[76]

Freedom of expression was
entrenched in our Constitution and is guaranteed in the
Quebec Charter
so as to
ensure that everyone can manifest their thoughts, opinions, beliefs, indeed all
expressions of the heart and mind, however unpopular, distasteful or contrary
to the mainstream. Such protection is, in the words of both the Canadian and
Quebec Charters, "fundamental" because in a free, pluralistic and
democratic society we prize a diversity of ideas and opinions for their
inherent value both to the community and to the individual.

Edmonton Journal v. Alberta
(A.G.)
:
[77]

It is difficult to imagine a
guaranteed right more important to a democratic society than freedom of
expression. Indeed a democracy cannot exist without that freedom to express new
ideas and to put forward opinions about the functioning of public institutions.
The concept of free and uninhibited speech permeates all truly democratic
societies and institutions. The vital importance of the concept cannot be
over-emphasized. No doubt that was the reason why the framers of the
Charter

set forth
s. 2
(b) in absolute terms which distinguishes it, for example, from

s. 8
of the
Charter
which guarantees the qualified right to be secure from
unreasonable search. It seems that the rights enshrined in
s. 2
(b) should
therefore only be restricted in the clearest of circumstances.

Hill v. Church of Scientology of
Toronto
:
[78]

Much has been written of the great
importance of free speech. Without this freedom to express ideas and to
criticize the operation of institutions and the conduct of individual members
of government agencies, democratic forms of government would wither and die.

R. v. Keegstra
:
[79]

The connection between freedom of
expression and the political process is perhaps the linchpin of the s. 2(b)
guarantee, and the nature of this connection is largely derived from the
Canadian commitment to democracy. Freedom of expression is a crucial aspect of
the democratic commitment, not merely because it permits the best policies to
be chosen from among a wide array of proffered options, but additionally
because it helps to ensure that participation in the political process is open
to all persons.

[
155
]

In my view, the more the remark bears on major political issues, the
broader the scope of freedom of opinion and freedom of expression becomes and,
proportionately, the more the protection guaranteeing the reputation of the individual
must yield.

[
156
]

The evidence heard in the present case strikingly illustrates the
appellant Lafferty’s poor knowledge regarding Nazism in general and Hitler in
particular, as well as his ignorance of both the political program of the Bloc
and Parti Québécois and the records in office of the respondents Parizeau and
Bouchard. The respondents see this ignorance as a decisive element in the
appellant’s liability for having dared to make such an odious comparison
without having investigated the facts to which he refers.

[
157
]

In my view, given the context and the circumstances, this element is
not sufficient. In the present case, when the respondents point out the
weakness of the factual basis on which the comparison is based, they are in
effect attacking the weak intellectual reasoning behind Lafferty’s remarks.
This alone is not sufficient to characterize the remarks as a fault. As Chief
Justice Dickson pointed out in
Keegstra
,
[80]
one of the objectives of freedom of
expression is “
to ensure that participation in the
political process is open to all persons.
” The
evidence proving the appellant’s ignorance simply demonstrates that his opinion
has limited value, not that he has committed a fault in expressing it.

[
158
]

It is not only scholars, intellectuals, the well-educated and the
well-informed who have the right to express their opinion freely on matters of
public interest. As long as the remarks do not contravene public order
provisions, in particular those found in the
Criminal Code
,
participation in political debate is open to all, even the ignorant and those
whose opinions are on the extreme ends of the ideological spectrum. In fact,
the protection of freedom of opinion and freedom of expression in the Charters
shows its true utility and value not when it ensures the free dissemination of opinions
on which there is a consensus, but rather when it prevents censorship and
repression of marginal opinions. On vitally important matters of public
interest, where is the outer limit of freedom of expression? What importance
should we assign to it? A quotation attributed to Voltaire
[81]
can give us an idea: [
translation
]:
“I disagree with what you say, but I will
defend to the death your right to say it.”

[
159
]

I am also in agreement with the following comment made by Mayrand
J.A. in
Dubois v. Société Saint-Jean-Baptiste
:
[82]

[
translation
]

One may not believe a single word
of the diatribe of the respondent, who may be mistaken, but this makes no
difference whatsoever. The respondent has the right to believe that the
appellants have betrayed the interests of Quebec, and if its belief is sincere,
it has the right to say it. The respondent would not be truly free to express
itself if it could only do so on the condition that it not make a mistake.

No one can deny that it expressed
itself in vehement – many would say shocking – terms. In a discussion of public
issues, however, where divergent political ideas clash, it is customary to use strong
and colourful language. The Courts are not mandated to impose standards of tact
or good taste. Through its aggressive tone and bold vocabulary, the respondent
may have approached the threshold of the intolerable, but has not stepped over
it.

[
160
]

Still within the framework of the contextual analysis, I observe
that the force of the comparison Lafferty makes and the vehemence and complete
lack of nuance in his remarks do not go beyond the boundary of usage one
observes in the political arena. In an article published in the 1999 edition of

Développements récents en droit municipal,
the author Denault discusses
the characteristics of confrontations in this area:
[83]

[
translation
]

It goes without saying that the
opinion that citizens have of a politician is of primordial importance. It is
also clear that the political milieu, because of the personal and collective
goals of those involved, is particularly fertile soil for strong emotions.
Indeed, the term “political arena” is apt, since an arena is the site of combat
and everything that this implies. No doubt it would be preferable if it were
not so, but it cannot be denied that strong language is a part of political
debate, and there is no indication that this will change in the foreseeable
future.

(Citations omitted)

[
161
]

Thibault J.A. makes the same observation in
Société
Saint-Jean-Baptiste de Montréal v. Hervieux-Payette
:
[84]

[
translation
]

There is no denying that some
politicians and political commentators do not mince words. Whatever the members
of this panel may think of the words used in the text cited above, the courts are
not arbiters in matters of courtesy, etiquette or good taste. Consequently, it
is not desirable for judges to apply the standard of their own tastes to censor
commentators, as that would spell the end of criticism in our society.

[
162
]

In this environment, participants rarely rely on subtlety. Rather,
their arsenals are filled with clear-cut and terse statements which, if taken
literally, could cause a person the loss of esteem or consideration. However,
unless there is a clear abuse of the freedom of expression, there is no call
for intervention. Forget J.A.’s comments regarding freedom of the press apply
in this case as well, with the necessary adaptations:
[85]

[
translation
]

I recall that in this case, we are
presented with a limit on the freedom of the press in the context of a
political debate, a freedom which must be restrained only in the most clear
cases, as Dickson C.J.C. points out in
Irwin Toy v. Attorney General of
Quebec
and Cory J. in
Edmonton Journal v. Alberta (Attorney General)

and
Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto
…

(Citations omitted)

[
163
]

In the context of political debate, a reasonable person hearing
accusations hurled back and forth between clashing opponents generally knows
enough not to take such comments at face value. As Chief Justice Tremblay
pointed out in the noted case
Hébert
,
[86]

an aggressive and hyperbolic style contains its own antidote.

[
164
]

In the present case, the evidence has shown that actors in the
political arena have made comparisons similar to those for which the appellant
is reproached. For example, around the time of the events that form the subject
matter of the present case, the media reported that the former premier of
Ontario, David Peterson, compared the exploitation and humiliation of Quebecers
by the respondent Bouchard to the exploitation and humiliation of Germans by
Hitler. In the October 6, 1993 edition of the daily newspaper the
Suburban
,
the following appeared:

Comparing the separatist movement
in Québec to that of the Nazi movement in Germany, former Ontario premier David
Peterson said there will always be tensions between Quebec and Ottawa as long
as separatists believe Quebec is being humiliated.

[
165
]

The
Globe and Mail
of October 9, 1993, reported the
following:

Former Ontario premier David
Peterson says Quebec separatism is based on the humiliation of the Quebec
people in the same way the Nazi movement built a powerful political force using
the humiliation of the German People.

On the television program
Fourth
Reading
on TVOntario Thursday night, Mr. Peterson said he saw a
parallel between the exploitation of emotions in Quebec by Bloc Québécois
Leader Lucien Bouchard and those feelings exploited by the Nazis in the wake of
Germany's First World War Defeat.

"If we want to build a whole
political structure on resentment and envy – and some people take advantage of
that – Bouchard's building his whole campaign on the basis of Quebec's
humiliation. I mean, I'll tell you another parallel of that, I mean Hitler
built the whole Nazi movement on the basis of the humiliation of Germany after
the First World War and built it into a political movement,"
Mr. Peterson said.

[
166
]

The lawyer Guy Bertrand, a person very present in the political
arena, also compared the politics of the Bouchard government with Nazi
theories, at least according to an article that appeared in
Le Devoir
on
December 3, 1997:

[
translation
]

The democracy of the Parti Québécois
is a popular dictatorship, states lawyer Guy Bertrand, who compares the
political philosophy of the Bouchard government with the theories that inspired
Adolf Hitler.

Speaking to a group of business
people yesterday in Montreal at a cocktail fundraiser to support his legal
action, the lawyer from Quebec City explained, “
Denying
the sovereignty of the courts and the citizens in the name of the will of the
people expressed by the National Assembly is equivalent to conferring total
power on the government. Since it is not tempered by the law, it is the law!
This type of dictatorship, authorized by the people, was used by the theorists
of the Third Reich to legitimate Hitler’s destruction of the German legal order
.”

[
167
]

Lafferty’s counsel rightly, in my opinion, affirm that the impugned
remarks were directed more at the doctrine of nationalism than at the
respondents themselves, which attenuates the injury somewhat. In the analysis,
we also observe that the respondents are not the primary targets of the
remarks, but that the defamation can be more accurately described as collateral
damage, to use a military term. Lafferty’s criticisms attack the entire
Canadian political system. His denunciation of nationalism, which by
association attacks the reputation of the respondents, is merely one element of
it.

[
168
]

The appellant also denied comparing the respondents themselves to
Hitler:

Q.    Okay. So accepting these as historical facts. I'm going to
quote a few sections of the official program of Adolf Hitler's party at the
time starting with
Article 4
.

A.     May I just intervene, I don't compare either Mr. Bouchard or
Mr. Parizeau to Hitler, I only say the policies which he followed… they
followed in terms of demagogy was similar to the policies which Hitler
followed.

[
169
]

If we rely on the
Globe and Mail
article submitted in first
instance, former premier David Peterson provided the same excuse to those who
perceived his remarks as drawing a parallel between Adolf Hitler and the
respondent Bouchard:

Of course, I'm not, I'm obviously
not. But I'm comparing a phenomenon on how you can use humiliation or slight or
the sense of abuse into an organized political movement.

[
170
]

In summary, when we consider the absence of malice and more specifically
the presence of good faith and sincerity  which  the trial judge explicitly
recognized, Lafferty’s liability for having expressed his opinion in the
context of a political debate can flow only from negligence or recklessness if
it is clear that he  expressed a totally inappropriate opinion. In my view,
this is where the boundary must be drawn to delineate the limits of freedom of
opinion and freedom of expression and to separate behaviour that is not
wrongful from that which is.

[
171
]

With respect for opinions to the contrary, I do not believe that the
respondents have established that Lafferty stepped over this limit. Certainly,
the conclusions he expressed appear extreme. However, we cannot ignore that the
bare facts could possibly lead a reasonable person to think of the comparison,
if only because it involves public figures who advocate, each in their way, the
values of belonging to a nation. Lafferty could have arrived at the conclusion
that the respondents’ nationalism differed in every way from that of the Nazis.
However, his natural aversion to the doctrine of nationalism prevented him from
making this distinction, and in fact led him to find parallels where very few
others see them. This does not, however, make the sincere and honest expression
of his conclusions an abuse of rights recognized by
section 3
of the
Quebec
Charter
.
[87]

[
172
]

Recently, although before the Supreme Court rendered its decision in

Prud’homme
,
[88]
a
majority of this Court
[89]

exonerated the Société Saint-Jean-Baptiste and some of its members, who had
published allegedly incendiary remarks regarding a number of federal members of
Parliament. The context of that case was analogous in that it too involved
remarks made in the context of participation in a democratic debate.

[
173
]

In my view, finding that Lafferty abused his freedom of expression
would be irreconcilable with the standard of conduct endorsed by this Court in
Hervieux-Payette.

The remarks analyzed in that case were, I believe, at least as virulent as the
ones in the present case. They were also ostensibly directed toward the
victims, like those which Lafferty made with respect to the respondents.

[
174
]

In first instance, the respondents convincingly established their
deep commitment to democratic values. As the evidence revealed, it was in this
regard that they felt the appellant’s remarks to be particularly unjust. A
large number of observers of the political scene shared this sentiment. The
only consensus the appellant’s opinion inspired was that expressed in the
general public denunciation of his remarks.

[
175
]

A few months after the incident, the majority of members elected to
the federal Parliament from the Province of Quebec were from Lucien Bouchard’s
party, in numbers sufficient to make him Leader of the Official Opposition. For
his part, in 1994, the respondent Jacques Parizeau was democratically elected
premier of Quebec.

[
176
]

I believe that the criticisms that were freely and publicly
expressed in support of the respondents and the popular vote in the two general
elections were a healthy counterbalance to the wrongs that the appellant could
have caused by his defamatory statements. Legal censure would bring about
nothing else than an inappropriate infringement on freedom of opinion and
freedom of expression.

[
177
]

I would therefore allow the appellants’ appeal with costs, set aside
the Superior Court judgment and dismiss with costs the respondents’ action in
defamation.
